sections.title: The Prohibition of Blood
sections.html:
Together with the permission to eat meat not in the framework of a sacrifice, we were forbidden to eat the blood, as it is stated (Devarim 12:20-23): "When the Lord your God shall enlarge your border, as He has promised you, and you shall say: I will eat meat… then you shall slaughter (tishḥat) of your herd and of your flock, which the Lord has given you, as I have commanded you, and you shall eat within your gates, after all the desire of your soul… Only be steadfast not to eat the blood, for the blood is the life (nefesh), and you shall not eat the life with the meat…" That is to say, blood has a special purpose – to sustain the life of the animal – and therefore, even though the Torah permitted us to eat meat, it did not permit eating the blood.

There are two kinds of blood: 'dam ha-nefesh' (life-blood) and the rest of the blood. 'Dam ha-nefesh' is the blood that gushes forcefully after the sheḥita, with which the soul departs; one who eats it intentionally is liable to karet, whereas one who eats of the rest of the blood is liable to lashes (Keritot 20b; SA 67:1). In 'dam ha-nefesh' the vitality of the animal is more prominent, and therefore when a sacrifice is offered, it is from this that one sprinkles on the altar in order to atone for the soul. It turns out that one who eats it also harms the honour of Heaven, for he eats the blood that was fit to be sprinkled on the altar. As it is stated in the section dealing with sacrifices (Vayikra 17:10-11): "And whatever man there be of the house of Israel, or of the strangers who sojourn among them, who eats any manner of blood, I will set My face against that soul that eats blood, and will cut it off from among its people. For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you upon the altar to make atonement for your souls; for it is the blood that makes atonement by reason of the life."

Since blood is meant to sustain the life of animals and not for human consumption, the Rishonim wrote that one who eats blood is liable to acquire beastly traits and the trait of cruelty in his soul (Ramban; Ḥinukh 148).1

sections.title: The Parameters of the Prohibition of Blood
sections.html:
The prohibition of blood applies to the developed species: domestic animals, wild animals and birds, as it is stated (Vayikra 7:26): "And you shall eat no manner of blood, whether of fowl or of beast (behema), in any of your dwellings"; the wild animal is included in "beast" (Keritot 21b). However, for the less developed species, such as fish and locusts, there is no prohibition of blood. That is to say, the prohibition of blood applies to the species that require sheḥita, and not to the species that do not require sheḥita. As we learned (above 18:11), one of the reasons for the mitzva of sheḥita is to minimise the suffering of the species whose meat we eat, and the mitzva applies to species whose brain and nervous system are more developed and which therefore also feel more pain. But the less developed species, such as fish and locusts, feel less pain, and therefore there is no obligation to slaughter them and no prohibition to eat their blood.

Blood that is absorbed in the meat in its natural way is permitted to be eaten. Therefore, it is permitted to eat a piece of raw meat. However, since when the meat is cut blood may ooze out at the place of the cut, one must rinse the place of the cut, and only afterwards is it permitted to eat it raw without further kashering (SA 67:1-2).2

When meat that has not been kashered is cooked, all of it becomes forbidden because of the blood that comes out of it during cooking and is absorbed in it again. And if this piece was cooked within a dish, since we have no ability to estimate how much blood is in it, we are stringent to regard all of it as blood, and as long as the dish does not contain sixty times its volume, the entire dish is forbidden (SA 69:11).3

Therefore, one must kasher meat before cooking it. However, according to the overwhelming majority of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim, kashering meat is meant to prevent a rabbinic prohibition, since blood that has been cooked or salted is forbidden only by the words of the Sages, because it has changed from its nature and is not fit to be sprinkled on the altar.4

sections.title: Methods of Kashering Meat from Blood
sections.html:
There are four methods of kashering meat from the blood in it: 1) salting,
2) roasting, 3) scalding in boiling water, 4) scalding in wine vinegar.

Salting and roasting are meant to draw the blood out of the meat. Salting does so by means of the salt, which draws the blood out of the meat. Likewise, roasting draws the liquids and the blood out of the meat and burns them. And indeed, even after salting or roasting has been completed, a red liquid still remains in the meat; however, according to halakha there is no prohibition in it, and it is not considered blood but 'ḥemar basar' (meat juice, literally "meat wine"). Moreover, even if we say that the salting or roasting did not succeed in drawing all the blood out of the meat, as long as the salting or roasting was carried out according to the law, there is no longer any prohibition on the red fluid that remains in the meat, and it is permitted to cook it, since it is impossible that the prohibition of blood should apply to blood that people cannot remove from the meat, for the Torah was not given to the ministering angels. In addition, according to the overwhelming majority of poskim, blood that has been salted or cooked is forbidden only by the words of the Sages, and they ruled that after proper salting or roasting, there is no longer any need to be concerned about the blood remaining in the meat, and if it flows out, it is permitted to eat it (Ran).5

In contrast to salting and roasting, which draw the blood out of the meat, scalding in boiling water or in vinegar is not meant to remove the blood from the meat but to seal it into the meat, so that the blood absorbed in the meat will no longer be able to move from its place even during cooking. And since there is no prohibition in blood that is absorbed in the meat, after scalding it is permitted to cook the meat.

However, the Geonim forbade kashering meat by scalding, lest the meat not be scalded properly. For scalding in boiling water depends on their succeeding in sealing the blood into the meat with a strong blast of heat; but if the water is not boiling enough, or if the meat is not put into the water all at once, or if the boiling water is a small quantity relative to the meat, it will not have the power to seal the blood into the meat. Likewise, regarding scalding in vinegar, there is a concern that the vinegar will not be strong enough for this. There is also a concern lest the vinegar turn slightly red, which is a sign that the scalding did not succeed and the meat and the vinegar have become forbidden, and perhaps they will not notice this (Ḥullin 111a; SA 67:5; 73:2). Therefore, one who wishes to cook meat must first kasher it by salting or roasting.6

sections.title: Preparing the Meat for Salting
sections.html:
Before we detail the order of salting with its three stages – rinsing, salting and rinsing – it should be prefaced that salting is effective for drawing out the blood absorbed in the meat, but is not effective for blood that is collected and visible inside the large blood vessels, such as those in the shoulder, the jaw and the tongue, since this blood is considered as collected and standing in a vessel. Therefore, one must cut them before salting, so that the blood collected in them can come out (SA 65:1). Salting is also not effective for the blood vessels in the membranes of the brain and in the testicles of the male, which must be removed, or at least cut, so that the blood in them can come out through salting (Ḥullin 93a).

Meat in which blood has collected because of a blow, to the point that it has turned red, must be cut before salting, in order to make an opening for the blood so that it can come out through it. And if after the salting the meat still remains red, there is no prohibition in this. When meat is kashered by roasting, there is no need to cut the meat, because roasting has the power to draw out collected blood without a cut (SA 67:4; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 16).

The Geonim ruled that salting is effective on condition that three full days (72 hours) have not passed over the meat from the time of the sheḥita. But if they have passed, there is a concern that the blood in the meat has dried to the point that salting does not have the power to remove it. It can then be kashered only by roasting, because whatever the roasting does not remove will not come out afterwards either. But ab initio one should not cook this roast, lest there remain in the meat blood that the roasting did not succeed in removing, and it will come out in cooking. After the fact, if it was cooked after roasting, it is kosher. In order not to come to a stumbling block and kasher by salting meat that has remained for three full days, it is proper to be careful not to leave meat for three full days (SA and Rema 69:12). Liver may be left, since in any case its kashering is by roasting only (Ḥamudei Daniel, cited in Pitḥei Teshuva 26).

If before three full days have passed over the meat it is soaked in water, this halts the process of the blood drying, and it will be permitted to kasher it by salting for another three full days. After the fact, if the blood vessels are removed from it, one may make do with rinsing the meat in order to permit its salting for another three full days (SA 69:13; Taz 33).

Some forbid leaving meat for three full days even when part of the time it is frozen, out of concern that even while it is frozen the blood dries and sticks to the meat (Yaskil Avdi part 1, YD 3; Shevet Ha-levi 2:25). However, in practice, since during freezing the blood does not dry but freezes, in a time of need one may freeze meat for many months and afterwards salt it, since the duration of the freezing is not counted towards the three full days (Arukh Ha-shulḥan 69:79; Yad Yehuda 59; Yabi'a Omer 2, YD 4; 7, YD 4).

As long as the meat is frozen, salting and roasting are not effective for it, because they cannot draw out the blood in it. To thaw it, it is permitted to soak it in warm water that is not yad soledet bo (hot enough that the hand recoils from it), but it is forbidden to soak it in water that is yad soledet bo, lest it cook the meat and cause the blood to be absorbed in it so that it becomes forbidden (Beit Yosef 69:1).

sections.title: Rinsing
sections.html:
There are three stages to kashering: rinsing, salting and rinsing, as the Sages said: meat is not freed of its blood unless one rinses it in water, salts it very well with salt, and again rinses it very well in water, in order to remove the salt with the blood in it (Ḥullin 113a).

There are several reasons for the rinsing before salting. First, in order to soften the meat, especially its surface, so as to allow the blood to flow out more easily (Ran and Haggahot Sha'arei Dura). Ab initio, so that the softening will be thorough, the custom is to soak the meat in water for half an hour. However, in a pressing situation, when there is no time for this, one may make do with a good rinse (Rema 69:1). In addition, if the meat is not rinsed of the blood on it, there is a concern that the salt will absorb the blood on the surface of the meat and will have no strength left to draw out the blood inside the meat (Ra'avya and Ra'avan).

A further reason: perhaps actual blood is stuck to the meat, and if it is not removed by rinsing, there is a concern that instead of the salt drawing the blood out of the meat, it will cause the blood on the surface of the meat to be absorbed into it with a power similar to cooking, since salt has the property that it sometimes cooks like something 'boiling' (below 35:8), and then the salting will no longer be able to remove the blood from the meat (Semag and Semak). However, in a pressing situation, meat that was salted without rinsing first is not forbidden; rather, one goes back, rinses it and salts it (SA and Rema 69:2).7

Before salting, one should wait until the water drips off the meat, for otherwise the water will dissolve the salt and it will run off the meat, and the salt remaining on the surface of the meat will not have the power to draw the blood out from within the meat. But it is forbidden to wait until the meat dries, because then the salt will not stick to the meat and will not be able to draw out the blood (Rema 69:1; Shakh and Taz).

sections.title: Salting
sections.html:
Salt is spread over the meat until no noticeable place on it remains without salt, and the meat is salted until it reaches a state in which, because of how salty it is, it would not be fit to eat; there is no need to add more than that.

The salt should be medium-grained, for if it is as fine as flour, there is a concern that it will be absorbed in the meat and lose its drawing power, and if it is very coarse, there is a concern that it will fall off the meat (SA 69:3). The recommended salt is called 'coarse salt for cooking'. After the fact, one may use even salt as fine as flour (Rema), and all the more so our regular salt, which is not as fine as flour.

The meat is salted on all its sides; after the fact, if the meat was salted on one side only and cooked, the meat is permitted. Salting all sides of the meat is not effective for the internal organs, each of which requires salting in its own right. Therefore, with a bird, the internal organs are taken out, and the bird is salted outside and inside, and the internal organs are salted separately on all their sides.8

The salted meat must be placed on a perforated vessel or on a tray placed at an incline, so that the blood that comes out of the meat will drip down or flow down the slope; for if it remains adjacent to the meat, there is a concern that it will be absorbed in it again, and there is also a concern that it will block the way for the blood still remaining in the meat to come out (SA 69:16-18).9

Ab initio, the meat should be left in the salt for an hour, and in a time of need one may make do with leaving it for eighteen minutes. And if the meat remained in its salt for less than eighteen minutes and was cooked, since blood still remained in it, the meat is forbidden to be eaten (SA 69:6; Rema 11; Taz 30).

Whether the piece of meat is as small as a kezayit or half a metre thick, the meat is left in its salt for the same length of time, for the Sages did not differentiate in their measures. For the salt draws out all the blood that can flow freely from it, and the liquids that are not drawn out of it, even though their colour is red, are not considered blood from the standpoint of halakha.10

One may salt many pieces of meat and place them in a pile one on top of the other until the blood comes out of them. And even if among them there are pieces of beef that exude a lot of blood and pieces of chicken that exude a little blood, there is no concern that the blood that came out of the beef will enter the chicken, because meat exudes its blood, or the brine that comes out of it, for twelve hours from the salting, and throughout that time it does not absorb blood that flows over it. And even if there is in the pile a piece that has a receptacle (a hollow) in which blood that flowed from other pieces collects, it does not become forbidden, and after the salting it is rinsed like the other pieces and is thereby kashered. However, ab initio a piece of meat that has a hollow should be placed facing downwards, so that blood that comes out during salting will not collect in it (SA and Rema 70:1, 5-6).

sections.title: The Rinsing after Salting
sections.html:
After the salting is completed, the meat must be rinsed in water; in practice the poskim ruled that the meat should be rinsed in water three times, each time in fresh water that has no remnants of blood in it. When the meat is rinsed under a stream of water from the tap, there is no need to do it three times; rather, it should be rinsed until not a trace of blood or salt remains on it.11

The salt with which the meat was salted, even if it has dried and it is not evident that blood is absorbed in it, is forbidden to be eaten, and one should not salt further meat with it (Rema 69:9).

Meat that was properly salted, and afterwards a red liquid flows out of it – from the standpoint of halakha this is not considered blood but 'ḥemar basar' (meat juice), that is, a red fluid that comes out of the meat. And even if the meat was cut and a red liquid flowed from the place of the cut, according to the overwhelming majority of poskim there is no prohibition in this liquid, since after salting all the red liquid remaining in the meat is fit to be eaten (as explained in note 5).

However, according to the Rambam (Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Asurot 6:10), salting is effective for removing the blood from the outer part of the meat only, but blood still remains in the inner part; therefore, after the second rinsing, the salted meat must be scalded by putting it into boiling water, so that all the blood that remains in it will be sealed in and stick to the meat and will no longer come out in cooking, and then it is dam evarim that has not separated, which involves no prohibition. And if the meat was not scalded in boiling water, the red liquid that comes out of it by itself or as a result of cutting the meat is forbidden as blood. And if the meat is cooked, the meat will become forbidden. But if after scalding a red liquid comes out of the meat, this is the fluid (mohal), which involves no prohibition.

In practice, the prevalent custom is not to be concerned for the opinion of the Rambam (Rema; Baḥ; Levush; Pri Ḥadash). Only among immigrants from Yemen are there some who are accustomed to be stringent according to his words. And some say that the Rambam's words were said regarding salting of eighteen minutes, but if the meat is left in the salt for an hour, as is customary today, all the blood comes out or is sealed into the meat, and even according to the Rambam there is no need afterwards to scald the meat in boiling water. And even if a red liquid flows out of it, there is no prohibition in it (Arukh Ha-shulḥan 69:36-40); and even those of Yemenite origin who are accustomed to be stringent and scald the meat may rely on this in a time of need.12

sections.title: Special Organs
sections.html:
Bones that contain marrow require 'rinsing, salting and rinsing' like meat, and the salting done on the bone is effective for the marrow inside. And if the meat was salted with the bones, the salting of the meat is effective for the bones as well (Rema 71:3; Shakh 11).

Heart: Blood is collected inside the chambers of the heart; therefore, one must first cut the heart and rinse out the blood remaining inside its chambers, and afterwards salt or roast it. After the fact, if the heart was salted or roasted without cleaning it, it should be cut and the blood collected in its chambers rinsed out (Mishna Ḥullin 109a; SA 72:1-2).

The intestines, from the stomach to the rectum, do not require salting, since they are not presumed to be organs that contain blood. That is, their blood is so slight that it is not noticeable, and there is no concern that it will leave its place. Only if there is a place in the intestines that has a red appearance – this indicates that blood has collected there and it must be salted. The fat on the intestines, like other fat and meat, requires salting. As for the rumen (keres), the reticulum (beit ha-kosot) and the omasum (hemses), even though some are lenient to regard them as included among the intestines that do not require salting (SA 75:1), in practice they must be salted like all meat (Rema; Pri Ḥadash; Maḥazik Berakha; Zivḥei Tzedek).

Liver and spleen: The liver is all blood, and therefore it is kashered only by roasting (below 12). The spleen, however, even though its colour is red like the liver, has the law of other meat, for which salting is effective. The spleen of a domestic animal must be peeled of the ḥelev attached to it (SA and Rema 74:1). And since peeling it involves great effort, the custom is not to kasher it but to sell it to non-Jews.

sections.title: The Question of Salt for the Ill
sections.html:
There are sick people for whom salt is harmful to their health, such as those suffering from high blood pressure, and for them eating meat that was properly salted is not healthy, because even though the salt is rinsed off the meat, part of it is absorbed in the meat and is dangerous for them. The first solution is to kasher the meat by roasting, since in this way there is no need to use salt. And even though ab initio the meat is salted a little before roasting, in a time of need one may be lenient about this (below, halakha 10). When the sick person cannot eat roasted meat, one may cook the meat after roasting in order to soften it.

Likewise, one may kasher a very large piece of meat by salting, and afterwards cut off the outer layer of the meat, in which the saltiness is perceptible, and give the sick person from the inner part, which has no saltiness.

When these solutions are not suitable, one may kasher the meat by scalding (above 3). True, the Geonim were stringent ab initio not to kasher by scalding; however, in a pressing situation they ruled to kasher the meat by scalding small pieces, taking care that before each piece is thrown into the water, the water boils and gives off steam (Knesset Ha-gedola and Maḥazik Berakha 69:51). And in this manner it is permitted to scald for the needs of a sick person (Yeshu'at Moshe 47; Shemirat Shabbat Ke-hilkhata 40:100; above, note 6).13

sections.title: Roasting
sections.html:
Just as salting kashers the meat by removing the blood, so roasting kashers the meat by removing the blood and burning it. And the power of roasting is greater than that of salting: salting is not effective for meat that has remained three days, because the blood in it has already dried, whereas roasting is effective for it (above 4). Likewise, salting cannot remove blood that has collected in the meat without cutting the place where it collected, whereas roasting removes it even without cutting the place where the blood collected (above 4). Salting is also not effective for the liver, since it is all blood, but roasting is effective for it (below 12).

This is the order of roasting: the meat is rinsed of the remnants of blood on it. Close to the roasting, it is desirable to salt it a little. It is roasted until it is fit to be eaten, and thereby it becomes kosher. In greater detail:

Before kashering the meat by roasting, it is rinsed of the blood on it, because some say there is a concern that perhaps the roasting will cause the blood on the meat to be absorbed into it. After the fact, if the meat was roasted without rinsing, as long as it is blood that came out of it, it is kosher. And if the blood on it came from other meat, the roast becomes forbidden (to the depth of a netila, or all of it, as cited in the note).

Ab initio, close to the roasting, a little salt is put on the meat, so that the salt will help the fire draw out the blood. And if salt was not put on, the meat is kosher. After salting the meat, it must be put on the fire immediately, for if the meat remains in its salt for several minutes, blood will begin to come out of it, and then it will be necessary to rinse the blood off the meat again before roasting. However, after the fact, if one forgot to rinse it, the roasting is valid, because roasting has the power to kasher the meat even while the blood that flowed from it is lying on it (SA and Rema 76:2).14

Some are accustomed to rinse the meat after roasting, to ensure that not a trace of blood remains on it (Rema 73:5; 76:2). However, when one wishes to eat the meat roasted and rinsing would spoil its taste, it is permitted to eat it without rinsing, for there is a presumption that the fire has burnt all the blood that came out of it.15

sections.title: The Measure of Roasting and Its Methods
sections.html:
The roasting that kashers the meat is roasting the meat until it would be fit, in a pressing situation, to be eaten by most people, which is the measure of half its roasting, that is, about half the time required for complete roasting, in which the roast becomes excellent and fit for all people. After that, even if a red fluid comes out of the meat, from the standpoint of halakha it is not considered blood but "ḥemar basar", that is, meat juice ("meat wine"), and it is permitted to eat it (Rema 76:2).

When one wishes to cook the roast, it is good to roast it completely.16

It is permitted and even desirable to turn the roast from side to side so that all of it will be roasted well. And one may turn it again several times. However, ab initio it is good to avoid rolling it continuously and quickly, because some are concerned that in this way the blood that came out of the meat will roll over it and be absorbed in it again (Rema 76:2; Minḥat Yaakov 9:6). But after the fact, if one did so, the meat is kosher, because even in this way the fire burns the blood that comes out of the meat (Yad Yehuda, Arokh 7).

It is permitted to roast many pieces of meat at once, and there is no concern that the blood that flows from the upper piece will be absorbed in the piece below it, since the property of blood that is drawn out of meat by roasting or salting is that it is 'mesharek sharik', that is, it slides off and is not absorbed.

When a large pile of pieces of meat is roasted at once, every piece that has become fit, in a pressing situation, to be eaten by most people is kosher. And one may take it out of the pile and eat it, even though there are still pieces above it and beside it that have not yet been kashered.17

sections.title: The Law of the Liver
sections.html:
The liver is full of blood, to the point that it was said of it that it is 'all blood'; nevertheless it is permitted to eat it, for the Torah forbade only blood that is poured out like water, and the liver is considered like congealed blood (Levush).

According to Rabbeinu Tam, a liver can be kashered by salting, except that since it is full of blood, before the salting one must cut it lengthwise and widthwise (crosswise), and place it with the cuts facing downwards, so that the blood in it will flow out of it. However, in practice it was ruled that a liver should not be kashered by salting, because the liver is full of blood, and salting does not have the power to remove from it all the blood required according to halakha. Therefore, only by roasting can a liver be kashered for eating, and after it has been properly roasted, it is permitted to cook it as well.

The large vessels in the liver should be cut before roasting it, so that the blood can flow out of them easily. In practice, since the gall bladder attached to the liver is cut off, the required opening is created, and therefore there is no obligation to cut further into the liver before roasting (and see the note).18

Ab initio, when roasting liver together with a piece of regular meat, one should not place the liver on the regular meat, since the liver has a lot of blood that will flow onto it. After the fact, the meat under the liver is kosher, since the abundant blood that comes out of the liver is 'mesharek sharik' (slides off) and is not absorbed in the piece beneath it, which is itself in the process of being kashered by the roasting (Ḥullin 111a; SA 73:4).

sections.title: The Fire and the Roasting Utensils
sections.html:
Roasting can be done over an open fire, when the meat is held on a grill or on a skewer and the blood that comes out of it flows into the fire. One may also roast meat by placing it directly on a plate heated by a fire burning beneath it or by electric heating elements beneath it. If the plate is smooth, the blood that comes out of the meat flows to the sides, and the little that remains under the meat is burnt up. But if it is rough or has depressions, it is proper to place it at an incline, so that the blood that comes out of the meat will flow downwards and not be trapped under the meat. It is forbidden to roast meat on a vessel or surface that has a receptacle, since the blood that comes out in roasting cannot flow to the sides and consequently will be absorbed in the meat and render it forbidden permanently, just as cooking meat that was not salted renders it forbidden permanently.19

It is permitted to roast meat inside a gas or electric oven, and it is permitted to close the oven during roasting. And it makes no difference whether the heating elements are under the meat, above it or beside it: as long as the meat is roasted properly and the blood has a place to flow, the meat is kashered. So that the bottom of the oven will not become dirty and even forbidden because of absorbing the taste of the blood, a vessel should be placed at the bottom of the oven to catch the blood that flows from the meat.20

Some are stringent not to cut with a knife meat that is on the fire before its kashering is complete, because the knife will absorb some of the blood and it will be necessary to kasher it by libun (heating to glowing) on the fire. And some are stringent and forbid the skewer on which the meat is roasted, because it absorbs some of the blood; therefore, before roasting further meat on it, it must be kashered by libun. And some are stringent and instruct to remove the meat from the skewer immediately after taking it off the fire, for otherwise there is a concern that the meat will absorb the taste of blood from the skewer.

However, in practice it was ruled in accordance with the permissive opinion in these three laws, since the act of roasting is a kashering, and if it kashers the forbidden meat, all the more so it does not render forbidden the utensils that touch the meat during the process of its kashering (Rosh; SA 76:4). True, some say that ab initio one should take into account the stringent opinion, and this is the custom of many of Ashkenazi origin. However, in practice, those of Ashkenazi origin too may be lenient in accordance with the majority of Rishonim, and use a skewer, a grill and a knife without libun.21

sections.title: The Blood of Fish, Locusts and Humans
sections.html:
The prohibition of blood applies only to species that, when they are pure, must be slaughtered in order for their meat to be permitted to be eaten, that is, species of domestic animal, wild animal and bird, and not fish and locusts (above, halakha 2). However, because of mar'it ayin (appearances), when it is not evident that it is the blood of fish or locusts, it is forbidden by the words of the Sages to eat it, lest people learn from this to eat forbidden blood. Therefore, when the blood of fish is collected in a vessel, it is forbidden by the words of the Sages to drink it, and only if it is evident that it is fish blood, such as when some scales or parts of fish were put in with it, is it permitted (SA 66:9). And if the blood of fish or of locusts became mixed into food, as long as it is not discernible – the mixture is permitted (Rema 66:10).

There is no Torah prohibition in eating human blood, but the Sages forbade eating human blood because of mar'it ayin. Therefore, one who bites into bread or an apple, and blood from his mouth remains on them, must scrape the blood off the bread or the apple, and afterwards he may continue to eat them. However, blood that comes out from between the teeth may be sucked, since it has not left the body, and there is no prohibition at all in it. Moreover, a person may suck blood that comes out of a finger, since it is evident that it is from the finger and not from a domestic animal or a bird (SA 66:10; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 47).
